section.title: Seek the LORD and Live
section.sectionRationale: The heart of the book. Amos raises a funeral song over Israel while she still lives, then presses the great gospel appeal, seek Me and live, three times over. He exposes the corruption of the courts, shatters the false hope of the Day of the LORD, and delivers God's stunning rejection of worship without justice, crowned by the book's most famous verse: let justice roll on like a river.
section.thesis: Israel is already as good as dead, yet the door of life stands open in the call to seek the LORD; and the God who is worshiped with songs He hates will accept nothing less than justice rolling like a river and righteousness like a never-failing stream.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the funeral lament; the threefold call to seek and live; the corruption of justice under the Creator's eye; the plea to seek good; the darkness of the Day of the LORD; and worship rejected in favor of justice.

units.label: A funeral song for the living

verses.text: Hear this word, O house of Israel, this lamentation I take up against you:
“Fallen is Virgin Israel, never to rise again. She lies abandoned on her land, with no one to raise her up.”

This is what the Lord GOD says: “The city that marches out a thousand strong will have but a hundred left, and the one that marches out a hundred strong will have but ten left in the house of Israel.”

units.label: Seek Me and live
units.note: not Bethel, not Gilgal, but the LORD

verses.text: For this is what the LORD says to the house of Israel: “{{darash|Seek}} Me and live!
Do not seek Bethel or go to Gilgal; do not journey to Beersheba, for Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.
Seek the LORD and live, or He will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph; it will devour everything, with no one at Bethel to extinguish it.

units.label: Justice turned to wormwood
units.note: the Maker of the Pleiades sees

verses.text: There are those who turn {{mishpat|justice}} into wormwood and cast {{tsedaqah|righteousness}} to the ground.
He who made the Pleiades and Orion, who turns darkness into dawn and darkens day into night, who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth, the LORD is His name,
He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold.
There are those who hate the one who reproves in the gate and despise him who speaks with integrity.

Therefore, because you trample on the poor and exact from him a tax of grain, you will never live in the stone houses you have built; you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted.
For I know that your transgressions are many and your sins are numerous. You oppress the righteous by taking bribes; you deprive the poor of justice in the gate.
Therefore, the prudent keep silent in such times, for the days are evil.

units.label: Seek good and live
units.note: hate evil, love good, establish justice

verses.text: Seek good, not evil, so that you may live. And the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed.
Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate. Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the {{sheerit|remnant}} of Joseph.”

units.label: The Day of the LORD is darkness

verses.text: Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of Hosts, the Lord, says: “There will be wailing in all the public squares and cries of ‘Alas! Alas!’ in all the streets. The farmer will be summoned to mourn, and the mourners to wail.
There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD.
Woe to you who long for the {{yom|Day of the LORD}}! What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light.
It will be like a man who flees from a lion, only to encounter a bear, or who enters his house and rests his hand against the wall, only to be bitten by a snake.
Will not the Day of the LORD be darkness and not light, even gloom with no brightness in it?

units.label: Let justice roll
units.note: worship God hates, justice God wants

verses.text: “I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies.
Even though you offer Me burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; for your peace offerings of fattened cattle I will have no regard.
Take away from Me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps.
But let {{mishpat|justice}} roll on like a river, and {{tsedaqah|righteousness}} like an ever-flowing stream.
Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You have taken along Sakkuth your king and Kaiwan your star god, the idols you made for yourselves.
Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus,” says the LORD, whose name is the God of Hosts.

darash.gloss: To seek, search out, resort to, inquire of. In this chapter it is God's central appeal, seek Me and live, and it is set against seeking the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal. To darash the LORD is to turn one's whole life toward Him for help and direction, and Amos insists that this seeking, not busy pilgrimage to false altars, is the path to life.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of life especially in the courts and toward the vulnerable. Israel turned mishpat into bitter wormwood, corrupting the gate where cases were heard. God's demand in verse 24 is that mishpat roll on like a river: not an occasional trickle of fairness but a flood that never dries up, carrying life to everyone in its path.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness, right relationship expressed in right conduct toward God and neighbor. Paired with mishpat, it describes a community shaped by God's own character. Israel cast tsedaqah to the ground; God wants it to flow like an ever-flowing stream, a wadi that, unlike the seasonal streams of the land, never runs dry even in the heat of summer.

sheerit.gloss: Remnant, remainder, what survives after disaster. Amos holds out a fragile hope: perhaps the LORD will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph. Judgment will fall, yet God may preserve a surviving few. This slender thread of the remnant runs through the prophets and is finally secured in Christ, in whom a people is saved out of the wreckage.

yom.gloss: The Day of the LORD, the day God decisively acts to judge His enemies and vindicate His people. Israel eagerly awaited it, assuming they were on the right side. Amos shatters that presumption: for an unrepentant covenant people the Day will be darkness, not light, like fleeing a lion straight into a bear. The Day is only good news for those who truly belong to God.

basic.context: This central chapter mixes lament, appeal, and warning. Amos sings a funeral song over Israel as if she has already fallen, yet three times he pleads, seek the LORD and live. He condemns bribed judges who crush the poor at the city gate. He warns those who long for the Day of the LORD that it will be darkness, not light. And he delivers God's shocking verdict: God hates their festivals and songs and wants instead justice rolling like a river and righteousness like a never-drying stream.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter holds together severe judgment and genuine invitation. Israel is as good as dead, yet the offer of life is real: seek God, not the shrines. The famous line about justice rolling down is not a rejection of worship as such, but of worship that coexists with injustice; God wants worshipers whose lives are just.
basic.originalLanguages: The pivotal verb is darash, to seek: seek Me and live. Israel had turned mishpat, justice, into bitter wormwood and cast tsedaqah, righteousness, to the ground; God wants both to flow unstoppably. He offers grace to a possible sheerit, a remnant. And He redefines the yom YHWH, the Day of the LORD, as darkness for the unrepentant.
basic.typology: The call to seek the LORD and live points to Christ, in whom God is truly found and life is truly given. The remnant God may spare finds its fulfillment in the people saved in Christ. And the demand for justice like a river anticipates the King whose kingdom is everlasting righteousness.
basic.christ: Seek Me and live is answered fully in Jesus, who says whoever comes to Him He will never cast out, and who is Himself the life. The Day of the LORD, darkness for the guilty, fell in its fullness on Christ at the cross, where the sun went dark at noon, so that for those in Him the Day becomes light. And the justice and righteousness God demands are both fulfilled and supplied in Christ.
basic.god: God is at once the righteous Judge who sings a funeral song over sin and the gracious Savior who pleads seek Me and live. He is the Creator who made the stars and rules the seas, so His moral demands carry cosmic weight. And He cares so deeply about justice that He will not accept worship offered by hands that oppress the poor.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 6:33 tells us to seek first God's kingdom and righteousness. Isaiah 1 shows God rejecting worship joined to injustice. Micah 6:8 sums up what God requires. Acts 7 cites Amos 5:25-27 in Stephen's sermon.
basic.oneStory: At the center of Amos stands both a funeral and an invitation: death for the impenitent, life for those who seek the LORD. The plea seek Me and live runs through Scripture to Christ, in whom God is found, the Day of darkness is borne, and justice at last rolls on like an unfailing river.

context.literary:
Amos 5 is built as a ring, and the hymn of verses 8 and 9 sits at its middle. Many readers see the funeral song of verses 1 to 3 answered by the exile of verses 25 to 27, the pleas to seek in verses 4 to 6 answered by the pleas to seek good in verses 14 and 15, and the charges of corrupt justice in verses 7 and 10 to 13 balanced by the woe over the Day of the LORD in verses 16 to 20. Whatever one makes of the symmetry, the placement of the hymn is deliberate. The One who 'turns darkness into dawn and darkens day into night' is introduced just before a people discover that the Day they wait for as light is dark. The same doxology style returns in Amos 4:13 and 9:5-6, so the book keeps stopping to remind its hearers who is speaking.

The opening is a qinah, the dirge sung at a burial, the form David used for Saul and Jonathan, 2 Samuel 1:17, and Ezekiel for the princes of Israel, Ezekiel 19:1. Amos sings it over a nation still walking about, and he does not hide that it is God's own word: verse 3 begins 'This is what the Lord GOD says,' and verse 4 begins 'this is what the LORD says.' The lament is not the prophet's mood but the Lord's verdict.

Notice how the speaker shifts. Verses 7 and 10 to 13 are third person accusation, 'there are those who,' as though Amos were speaking of absent criminals. Verses 14 and 15 swing to second person imperatives, so the guilty are suddenly addressed, and the exhortation is aimed at those who can still act. Each 'Therefore' (verses 11, 13 and 16) marks a consequence drawn from a charge. And the chapter closes with the hardest turn of all: the rhetorical question of verse 25 and an exile that the LORD, 'whose name is the God of Hosts,' announces in verse 27, so that the title which opened the book of hope in verse 14 now seals the sentence.
context.historical:
The gate was the Israelite town's court, council chamber and market in one, and verses 10 to 12 show it from the inside. The elders sat there to hear lawsuits, and the one who 'reproves in the gate' is the honest arbiter or witness who will not bend the case. Exodus 23:6-8 had warned judges against denying the poor their rights and taking bribes, because a bribe 'blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous,' and Isaiah 29:21 describes the same scene, men who 'ensnare the mediator at the gate' and 'deprive the innocent of justice.' When Amos says that the poor were 'deprived of justice in the gate,' he is describing the collapse of the one institution that was supposed to protect them.

The 'tax of grain' of verse 11 points to the economic engine behind this. Under the long, prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, 2 Kings 14:25-28, wealth gathered in the hands of a few landholders, while small farmers fell into debt and paid their rents in grain. The stone houses and lush vineyards of the elite were built on that harvest. Amos answers in the language of the covenant curses: 'You will build a house but will not live in it. You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit,' Deuteronomy 28:30. The people who thought themselves blessed had walked into the curse.

The three shrines of verse 5 mark the geography of popular religion. Bethel held a calf shrine since the first Jeroboam, 1 Kings 12:28-29, Gilgal was a place of ancient memory, and Beersheba lay far to the south in Judah, so that pilgrims were willing to cross a border for the sake of a holy site. Amos plays on their names: Gilgal will 'surely go into exile,' the verb echoing the town's name, and Bethel, 'house of God,' will come to nothing, the word in the footnote being Aven, 'a derogatory term for Bethel; see Hosea 4:15.' Verses 25 to 27 touch a more difficult scene. The Hebrew names Sakkuth and Kaiwan are generally taken as astral deities from Mesopotamia, and the Greek translation reads differently, as the BSB footnote observes: 'the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan.' Whatever the original behind those words, the charge is the same, that Israel's worship had long been mixed with the worship of the sky.
context.canonical:
Amos 5:24 has had an enormous afterlife. It is one of the most quoted lines in the Bible in movements for civil rights and social reform, and Martin Luther King Jr. quoted it in his Birmingham jail letter and the I Have a Dream speech. But it first lived inside Scripture, where the critique of empty worship is one of the prophets' steady themes. Isaiah 1:11-17 speaks of sacrifices and festivals God cannot endure and includes the call to 'seek justice and correct the oppressor.' Hosea 6:6 says 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' and Jesus twice quotes it against religious leaders, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7. Micah 6:6-8 asks whether rams and rivers of oil will do, and answers 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.' Jeremiah 7:21-23 says that God never based the covenant on burnt offerings but on obedience.

The invitation to seek and live has its own line of descent. Moses set 'life and death' before Israel and said 'choose life,' Deuteronomy 30:19, Ezekiel heard God say 'I take no pleasure in anyone's death... So repent and live,' Ezekiel 18:32, and Isaiah called out 'Seek the LORD while He may be found,' Isaiah 55:6.

The Day of the LORD is picked up by those who follow Amos. Joel 2:1-2 calls it 'a day of darkness and gloom,' and Zephaniah 1:14-15 describes the 'great Day of the LORD' as 'a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness.' In the New Testament Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 in Acts 7:42-43, adapting 'beyond Damascus' to 'beyond Babylon' to match the exile that actually came. James and John carry the justice theme forward: faith that does nothing for the hungry is dead, James 2:14-17, and love must be 'in action and truth,' 1 John 3:18. The river of verse 24 finds its last form in 'a river of the water of life' flowing from the throne of God, Revelation 22:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos wanted two groups of hearers to feel two different things. For the comfortable, the funeral song was meant to shock: a nation that cannot imagine itself dying is told that the body is already on the bier. For anyone still listening, the repeated 'seek' was a real exit. He pointedly offers no third way. The people could not seek the LORD at Bethel while crushing the poor at the gate, and they could not claim that the LORD was 'with' them, as verse 14 notes they did, while despising the one who spoke honestly.

He also meant to take apart a slogan. 'The LORD is with us' was the popular creed, and Amos accepts the words but not the way they were used. God is with those who seek good, he says, and the 'perhaps' of verse 15 is there to forbid taking His presence for granted. Grace is not something they hold in reserve but something they can only ask for.

For later readers, especially those carried into exile, the chapter was meant to make sense of catastrophe. The funeral song they remembered had been sung while the nation was healthy. Those who survived would know it had not been the prophet's cruelty but God's warning, and the remnant of verse 15 would see that the door of life had been held open until the last.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 13 is description, not advice. 'The prudent keep silent in such times' reports what happens in an unjust city, where wisdom becomes self-protection, and it should not be read as a recommendation to stay quiet when truth is unwelcome. The prescriptions are in the commands around it: seek the LORD, seek good, hate evil, love good, establish justice in the gate. Those verbs fall most heavily on people who held a seat at the gate, the judges, landholders and officials, and for us they apply wherever we have a voice or a vote in the courts, councils, workplaces and households that shape the lives of others.

Verses 21 to 23 do not abolish worship. The feasts, assemblies and offerings listed were commanded in the Law, and the same Amos calls God's people to seek Him. The prescription is that worship must not be used as a cover for oppression, a way of buying peace with God while ignoring the poor. And the picture of the Day of the LORD, verses 18 to 20, is a warning aimed at the confident, not a forecast of what awaits every believer. Those who truly seek the LORD have nothing to fear from the Day, but those who treat God's favour as a possession must reckon with it.

debates.question: Does Amos 5:21-24 reject sacrificial worship itself, or only worship cut off from justice?

views.label: A rejection of empty ritual, not of worship
views.case: God instituted the feasts and offerings He here refuses, and the same chapter tells Israel to seek Him. The accusation is against worshippers whose hands are unjust. This reading fits the parallel passages in Isaiah 1:11-17 and Micah 6:6-8, where the offerings are condemned alongside the oppression that accompanies them.

views.label: A radical prioritising of justice over ritual
views.case: The language is sweeping: 'I hate, I despise,' 'I will not accept them,' 'I will not listen.' Jeremiah 7:22 says God did not merely command burnt offerings but obedience, and Hosea 6:6 sets mercy against sacrifice. On this view justice is not an addition to the cult but its test, and God counts any worship without it as noise.

views.label: A call to a different kind of worship
views.case: Some argue that the picture is of a cult that had become a stage for national pride and a way of appeasing God, so Amos is not subtracting liturgy but replacing its purpose: God does not need sacrifices to survive, and the relationship they were meant to express is the thing He wants. The river of verse 24 is the true offering.

debates.bearing: All three agree that God will not be worshipped by unjust hands. Worship and justice are inseparable, and the verse works best as a test for every act of devotion: does it flow into righteousness for the weak, or does it stand in place of it?

debates.question: Did Israel really offer no sacrifices in the wilderness, verse 25?

views.label: The question expects the answer no
views.case: Read literally, 'Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness?' seems to deny that Israel brought offerings. On this view God's point is that the covenant at Sinai began with obedience, as Jeremiah 7:22-23 says, and that sacrifices were not the foundation of the relationship.

views.label: The question expects yes, but not to Me alone
views.case: Numbers records offerings in the wilderness, so the question may stress that those offerings were mixed with devotion to other gods, as the next verse suggests. Stephen reads it this way in Acts 7:42, where God 'gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven.' The sentence then means that they offered, but not to Him alone.

views.label: A rhetorical question about the proper order
views.case: Others take it as a way of saying that sacrifice, in the age of the wilderness, was never the heart of things; mercy and justice preceded and defined the sacrificial system, and the point of verse 25 is about what is primary, not what was absent.

debates.bearing: The first and third views fit the force of verses 21 to 24, and the second fits Stephen and the idolatry of verse 26. In each case the lesson is the same: what God seeks is a people who belong to Him wholly, and offerings given in place of loyalty are worth nothing.

debates.question: What is the 'silence' of the prudent in verse 13?

views.label: Sad realism
views.case: Amos notes what happens in an unjust city: the shrewd keep their heads down because honest speech, as verse 10 reports, is hated at the gate. The verse is a grim description of a society in which wisdom has become survival.

views.label: Bitter irony
views.case: Others hear mockery. The 'prudent' who stay silent are condemned as much as the judges, since silence in the face of oppression is complicity, and the verse is meant to shame the sensible as well as the corrupt.

views.label: A reference to wise silence before judgment
views.case: Because 'the days are evil,' silence may also be what remains once God is about to act, as in Amos 8:3, where corpses lie strewn 'in silence everywhere.' On this reading the verse is a foretaste of the hush of a doomed city.

debates.bearing: The verse is no endorsement of silence. The commands of verses 14 and 15, to seek good and establish justice in the gate, are the exact opposite of the quiet it describes.

study.originalLanguages:
The word translated 'wormwood' in verse 7, laanah, names a bitter plant, and Scripture uses it for what is poisonous to the soul. Deuteronomy 29:18 warns of a 'root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit,' the idolatrous heart that turns from the LORD, and Jeremiah 9:15 threatens to feed the people wormwood. The verb Amos pairs with it matters more. Those who 'turn' justice into wormwood use the verb hafakh, to overturn or reverse, the verb that describes Sodom's overthrow, as in Genesis 19:25 and Amos 4:11, and in verse 8 it describes the LORD who 'turns darkness into dawn.' Only God may turn darkness to morning. Those who turn justice into bitterness are practising in the moral world what God did to Sodom in the physical world, and Amos 6:12 repeats the charge, 'you have turned justice into poison.'

The 'ever-flowing' stream of verse 24 translates two words, nachal and eitan. A nachal is a wadi, the seasonal riverbed of Israel's hills, which roars in winter and cracks in the dry months. Eitan means permanent or perennial, and it is used elsewhere of rivers that never dry, Psalm 74:15. So Amos asks for a wadi that does not fail. The verb 'roll,' from galal, is the verb for rolling a great stone, as the shepherds roll away the stone from the mouth of the well in Genesis 29:3. The mild English word hides a note of force: justice is meant to move like something heavy and unstoppable, carrying away whatever blocks it.

The phrase 'I cannot stand the stench' in verse 21 uses a verb for smelling, the verb used when 'the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma' of Noah's offering, Genesis 8:21. Leviticus 26:31 uses it in the covenant curse: 'I will refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices.' The 'pleasing aroma' of the altar becomes something God will not breathe in. The 'noise' of the songs in verse 23, hamon, is a word for a crowd's roar or tumult, so what should have been music reaches God as din.

The 'perhaps' of verse 15, ulai, is a word of hope without a guarantee. Moses uses it when he goes up to plead for the golden calf worshippers, 'perhaps I can make atonement,' Exodus 32:30, and the king of Nineveh and Joel 2:14 use a different idiom of the same kind, 'Who knows?' Prophets use this idiom when they hold out repentance without turning it into a contract. God is not bound by Israel's repentance, and yet repentance is the only door.

The 'Virgin Israel' of verse 2 uses betulah, the title of a young woman not yet a mother. The same name appears in Jeremiah 31:4, 'Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel.' The fallen girl who had a future cut off is the same girl Jeremiah sees rebuilt, and the verb 'rise,' qum, in 'never to rise again' is the verb Amos will use in 7:2, 'How will Jacob survive?', and in 9:11, where God promises to raise up David's fallen tent.

Verse 26 is textually difficult. The Hebrew names are Sakkuth and Kaiwan, and the Septuagint, followed by Stephen in Acts 7:43, reads 'Molech' and 'Rephan,' so that translators cannot be sure whether Amos names two gods, or two titles, or an idolatrous procession. Either way the verse speaks of idols 'you made for yourselves.'

typology.type: The funeral song over Virgin Israel, Amos 5:1-3
typology.fulfillment: A dirge sung over the living ends with the haunting line 'no one to raise her up.' The answer arrives in the gospel's central act. Paul says God 'made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses' and 'raised us up with Christ,' Ephesians 2:5-6, and Jesus Himself wept over Jerusalem in the same mood of foreboding, Luke 19:41-44. What Israel could not do for herself, resurrection does. The type falls short in that Amos's lament was sung over a nation, while the raising Christ gives is personal and still awaits its completion at the last day.

typology.type: Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba against the LORD Himself, Amos 5:4-6
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told to seek a Person, not a place. Bethel had once been the 'house of God' where Jacob saw the gate of heaven, Genesis 28:17, but it had become a king's shrine. Jesus tells Nathanael that he would see 'heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man,' John 1:51, taking to Himself the Bethel vision, and He tells the woman at the well that true worshippers will worship 'in spirit and in truth,' John 4:21-24. The shrines fall away because the One they pointed to has come.

The river of justice that never runs dry pictures what only God can supply. Ezekiel's vision of water flowing from the temple and deepening with each measure, Ezekiel 47:1-9, and Jesus' invitation, 'Streams of living water will flow from within him,' John 7:37-38, carry the image forward, and Revelation 22:1 sets 'a river of the water of life' flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The river is no longer a demand placed on a failing people but a gift flowing from the throne. The type is not completed until the new creation.

typology.type: The Day of darkness and not light, Amos 5:18-20
typology.fulfillment: Amos prepares an unwelcome answer: the Day will be gloom. Christ takes this darkness on Himself when 'darkness came over all the land' at the cross, Mark 15:33, a darkness Amos 8:9 had foretold when the Lord said He would make 'the sun go down at noon.' The New Testament does not claim Amos was predicting Calvary in detail, so this is an echo and not a quotation, but the pattern holds. The One who is Himself 'the light of the world,' John 8:12, enters the darkness so that those in Him need not.

A 'perhaps' hope for a remnant is carried on in Paul's teaching that 'at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5. The remnant of Amos is a handful spared out of judgment; in Christ the remnant becomes the nucleus of a people gathered from every nation. The type falls short because Amos speaks only of Israel, while Paul sees the remnant's calling opened to Jew and Gentile alike.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by its invitation. 'Seek Me and live' receives a face in Jesus, who says that 'the one who comes to Me I will never drive away,' John 6:37, and 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. The 'perhaps' of verse 15 is the part that changes most. Amos could only say that God might be gracious; Jesus is the place where the grace has been decided. 'I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness,' John 10:10.

It leads to Christ by the problem it exposes. If God hates worship that tolerates injustice, and if the Day of the LORD is darkness, then no one in Israel, and no one at all, is able to seek good as the verse demands. Paul answers that 'the righteousness of God has been revealed' and that God acted 'to demonstrate His righteousness' so as 'to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:21-26. Justice and righteousness, the two words Amos wants to see rolling, are exactly the two things God secures at the cross. Justice is done because sin is judged, and righteousness is given to all who trust Him.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the temple. Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 to those who thought their religion was enough, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Matthew 9:13, and He overturns the tables in the temple court, Matthew 21:12-13. He does not cancel worship. He fulfils it, and He gathers a people whose worship cannot be separated from mercy, as the Sermon on the Mount makes clear in 'seek first His kingdom and His righteousness,' Matthew 6:33.

It leads to Christ in the darkness. Amos 5:18 warns that the Day is darkness, and Amos 8:9 announces a darkened sun at noon. The darkness that fell over the land while Jesus hung on the cross, Matthew 27:45, is the Day's gloom borne by the One who 'knew no sin,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, so that those who come to Him pass through the Day into the light, John 8:12.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Amos is not talking about the cross in chapter 5, and he does not name the Messiah. What he supplies is the question to which Christ is the answer: how can a God who hates injustice receive unjust people, and who will raise the fallen Virgin? The New Testament's answer is in a death and a resurrection, and the chapter's reversal of every false hope prepares us to receive it.
study.god:
The hymn at the heart of the chapter tells us who is making the demands. He 'made the Pleiades and Orion,' Job 9:9 uses the same pair, He turns darkness into dawn, and He pours the sea over the earth. The LORD of the constellations is also the LORD of the courtroom, and Amos does not let the two be separated. Cosmic power is not a distraction from social justice but its guarantee: the One who rules the stars notices the bribe taken at the gate.

He is a God who knows. 'For I know that your transgressions are many and your sins are numerous,' verse 12, and the specific list that follows, bribes, taxes on the poor, silenced witnesses, shows that His knowledge is not general but exact. He also knows the poor man's lawsuit and the judge's price.

He feels. 'I hate, I despise... I cannot stand.' The words are not moral tut-tutting but the revulsion of a holy God, and they show that He is moved by what happens in His creation. Yet the same God says 'Seek Me and live,' so His holiness and His mercy are not opposites. The wrath of verses 5 and 6 and the invitation of verses 4 and 14 come from the same character.

He is the God of the Exodus, and verse 17 reverses it. 'I will pass through your midst,' He says, and the phrase is the one used of the night in Egypt, 'I will pass through the land of Egypt,' Exodus 12:12. In Egypt the LORD passed through to judge and passed over the houses marked by blood, Exodus 12:23. Now He promises to pass through Israel's own vineyards, and no blood is on the doorframe. The God who saved His people will not spare those who have become like Egypt.

He is free. The 'perhaps' of verse 15 and the three-fold 'live' tell us He cannot be manipulated by ritual or demanded of by ancestry, and yet He is not capricious. His name, 'the LORD, the God of Hosts,' occurs repeatedly in the chapter, in verses 14, 15, 16 and 27, as a title of the commander of heaven's armies, and the hymn of verse 8 ends with 'the LORD is His name,' as though the whole argument rested on knowing who is speaking.

For worship, the chapter forces a question each time we gather: is what we bring to God joined to what we do on Monday? The God who hates the noise of songs sung over injustice is the God who, in Christ, delights in a people whose lives are lined with mercy, and who still says, to the weakest of them, 'Seek Me and live.'

crossReferences.note: Moses sets before Israel 'life and death, blessing and cursing' and says 'choose life.' Amos's threefold 'seek and live' is the same choice offered again to a nation near the end of its patience. Life in both places means the covenant relationship with the LORD, not mere survival.

God says through Ezekiel that He takes no pleasure in anyone's death and calls the house of Israel to 'repent and live.' This shows that the funeral song of Amos 5:1-3 is not God's wish for His people but the outcome He pleads with them to avoid.

The nearest parallel to Amos 5:21-24. God asks what good is a multitude of sacrifices and says He hates the New Moons and feasts, then tells the worshippers to 'seek justice, correct the oppressor,' and defend the fatherless. Together the two passages show how consistent the prophets were on this point.

'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' Hosea, Amos's northern contemporary, puts the same truth as a principle, and Jesus later quotes it twice, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, to show that the heart of the Law was never the ritual alone.

Micah asks what to bring before the LORD, with year-old calves or ten thousand rivers of oil, and answers 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.' It reads like a summary of Amos 5, and shows what 'justice rolling like a river' looks like in a single person's life.

God says that when He brought Israel out of Egypt He did not merely command burnt offerings but obedience. This is the closest commentary on Amos 5:25, since both passages say that the sacrificial system was never what the relationship was built on.

The covenant curse of building a house without living in it and planting a vineyard without enjoying its fruit is exactly what Amos 5:11 announces. The prophet is not inventing a new judgment but reading Israel the sentence they had agreed to at Sinai.

The LORD says, 'I will pass through the land of Egypt.' Amos 5:17 uses the same wording, 'I will pass through your midst,' so that Israel, who once sheltered from the destroyer by blood, now stands where Egypt stood. It is one of the great reversals in the prophets.

Zephaniah develops the idea of Amos 5:18-20, calling the great Day of the LORD 'a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness.' The warning that the Day is not simply good news for Israel became fixed in the prophetic tradition.

Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 in his sermon to show that idolatry was part of Israel's story from the wilderness. He follows the Greek text, which reads Molech and Rephan, and he writes 'beyond Babylon' where Amos has 'beyond Damascus,' since by his day the exile had gone further.

'Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness.' Jesus draws on the same seeking-and-living logic: those who put God and His righteousness first are the ones who find that everything else is given. It is the New Testament face of 'Seek the LORD and live.'

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side. What Amos asked to roll like a river on earth is seen finished in the new creation, where the justice and righteousness of God are no longer demanded but supplied.

study.oneStory:
Amos 5 stands in the middle of the story's great collision: a holy God who made everything good, and a people who have turned justice into poison. From the garden onward the Bible asks whether life is possible once trust has been broken. Here Israel is the test case. They have the covenant, the land, the shrines, the feasts and the name of the LORD on their lips, and still they are, in the prophet's word, fallen. The chapter shows that religion cannot repair what has gone wrong with the human heart.

It also draws on what went before. The covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28 hangs over verse 11, the Exodus lies behind verse 17, and Moses's 'choose life' stands behind the threefold 'seek and live.' The God who spoke from Sinai is the God who now sings the funeral song, and the offer of life has not changed.

It sets up what follows. The exile of verse 27 happens, and the northern kingdom falls. Yet the 'perhaps' of verse 15 and the remnant of Joseph point beyond it, and the book ends not with a funeral but with the promise to 'restore the fallen tent of David,' Amos 9:11. The question 'who will raise her up?' is answered by the prophets who later promise 'Again I will build you,' Jeremiah 31:4, and finally by Christ, who makes the dead alive, Ephesians 2:5.

The pieces come together in Jesus. He is the One in whom God is found, the One who carries the Day of darkness, and the One who gives the righteousness that Israel could not produce. In Him, justice and righteousness are both satisfied and given, and a people who have been made alive by grace are sent to be what Amos asked for, a community in which justice flows.

The story ends in a city where the river no longer needs to be demanded. In Revelation 22:1-2 the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the tree of life bears its fruit, and the nations are healed. The funeral song becomes a wedding feast, and what Amos called for from the gate of a failing town is finally given to the whole creation.

quiz.q: How can Amos sing a funeral song over Israel and still say seek Me and live?

options.text: Israel is as good as dead under judgment, yet God genuinely holds open the door of life to those who turn and seek Him.
options.note: Judgment and real invitation stand together in the chapter.

options.text: The funeral song is only symbolic and there is no real danger.
options.note: The threat of death is real; so is the offer of life.

options.text: God laments the coming ruin but still offers a way to live.
options.note: Right about both; the sharp point is that Israel is already as good as dead, yet life is offered.

options.text: God changed His mind and cancelled the judgment.
options.note: The judgment stands; life comes through seeking Him, not through its cancellation.

quiz.q: What does God mean by let justice roll on like a river and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream?

options.text: He wants constant, life-giving justice and righteousness that never dry up, not an occasional trickle of fairness.
options.note: The ever-flowing stream never fails, even in summer drought.

options.text: He wants Israel to build irrigation for their crops.
options.note: The river is a metaphor for enduring justice and righteousness.

options.text: He wants justice and righteousness to flow through the community.
options.note: Right, and the image stresses that it must be constant and never-failing.

options.text: He wants occasional acts of charity when convenient.
options.note: The picture is a flood that never dries up, not occasional charity.

quiz.q: Why does God say He hates Israel's feasts and songs?

options.text: Because worship offered by people who oppress the poor is offensive to Him; He will not be worshiped by unjust hands.
options.note: Worship and justice are inseparable in God's sight.

options.text: Because God dislikes music and festivals in general.
options.note: God instituted these feasts; the problem is injustice, not worship itself.

options.text: Because their worship was disconnected from just living.
options.note: Right, and God's language shows how deeply such hollow worship offends Him.

options.text: Because they used the wrong instruments.
options.note: The issue is the injustice behind the worship, not the instruments.

quiz.q: Why does Amos say the Day of the LORD will be darkness, not light?

options.text: Israel presumed the Day would crush their enemies, but as God's unrepentant people they themselves face judgment.
options.note: The Day is only good news for those truly on God's side.

options.text: Because it will literally be a cloudy day.
options.note: Darkness here means judgment, not weather.

options.text: Because they were wrongly confident they were safe on that Day.
options.note: Right about false confidence; specifically their own sin makes the Day dark for them.

options.text: Because the Day of the LORD is always bad for everyone.
options.note: For the faithful the Day is light; it is darkness for the impenitent.

quiz.q: How does the Day of the LORD as darkness point to Christ?

options.text: The darkness of judgment fell on Jesus at the cross, so that for His people the Day becomes light.
options.note: The sun darkened at noon as Christ bore the day of judgment.

options.text: It simply warns us to be ready for the end of the world.
options.note: True in part, but Scripture ties the darkness specifically to the cross.

options.text: It shows Jesus also spoke about a coming day of judgment.
options.note: Right that Jesus taught it, but the deeper link is that He bore the darkness for us.

options.text: It has no relationship to Jesus.
options.note: The New Testament connects the Day and the darkness directly to Christ.

questions: Three times God pleads, seek Me and live. What are the Bethels and Gilgals, the substitutes for God, that you find yourself seeking instead of Him?
God will not accept worship from hands that oppress the poor. Is there any injustice in your life or dealings that makes your worship hollow?
Justice was meant to roll like a river that never dries up. Where is God calling you to move from occasional fairness to steady, flowing righteousness?
Israel wrongly assumed the Day of the LORD would be light for them. Where might you be presuming on God's favor without truly seeking Him?
Jesus bore the day of darkness so it could become light for His people. How does that turn your dread of judgment into confidence, and gratitude?

translationNotes.note: Bethel will come to nothing renders a Hebrew wordplay: Bethel, house of God, becomes Beth-aven, house of nothing or house of wickedness, a derogatory nickname also used in Hosea.
Ever-flowing stream translates nachal ethan, a wadi that keeps running even in the dry season, unlike the many seasonal streams of the land; the image stresses justice that never fails.
Sakkuth and Kaiwan are astral deities; the Septuagint renders them differently, and Stephen follows that reading when he cites the passage in Acts 7:42-43.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Amos 5:1-27. Poetic line fragments joined into running verse text; footnote markers omitted; Tokens for justice and righteousness placed at both verse 7 and the climactic verse 24.
